This is a Gaussian product kernel: each component has its own bandwidth, so the data can decide that, for example, the level relative to the maximum must match closely while growth may differ more. The hard restriction to origins within 4 weeks, on top of the kernel in `season_week`, keeps the analogs at a similar stage of the season and limits computation. The source factor is the kernel of Aitchison and Aitken (1976) for a categorical variable, it equals 1 for the same source and $\lambda$ for a different one.

### Weighted analog predictive distributions

The weighted analog outcomes define a joint predictive distribution of $(k^+, z)$ (a Nadaraya–Watson-type estimator of a conditional distribution; Hyndman, Bashtannyk and Grunwald 1996), whose two marginals are used:

- **timing:** $\pi^{\text{A}}_j(\phi) = \sum_i \varpi_i(\phi)\, \mathbf{1}\{k^+_i = j\}$, $j = 0, \dots, k_{\max}$. KCDE uses the exact offsets, without grouping into a tail class.
- **size:** the weighted empirical distribution function $F^{\text{A}}(v \mid \phi) = \sum_i \varpi_i(\phi) \mathbf{1}\{z_i \le v\}$, whose atom at zero comes from analogs that had already peaked.

### Mixing with the baseline

Analog methods fail badly when the current season looks unlike anything in the history, because the weights then concentrate on a few poor analogs. To guard against this, the forecast is a mixture with the baseline of @sec-baseline, fitted to the same training rows, with weight $\eta$:
$$
\pi_j = (1 - \eta)\, \pi^{\text{A}}_j + \eta\, \pi^{\text{base}}_j, \qquad F = (1 - \eta) F^{\text{A}} + \eta F^{\text{base}}.
$$
For size, the mixture is computed on discretized versions of the two distributions. The analog distribution is represented by its weighted quantiles $q^{\text{A}}(\tau') = \inf\{v : F^{\text{A}}(v \mid \phi) \ge \tau'\}$ on the 99-level grid $\tau' \in \{0.01, 0.02, \dots, 0.99\}$, each given mass $(1-\eta)/99$; the baseline by its 23 quantiles $q^{\text{base}}(\tau)$, each given mass $\eta/23$. The output quantile at level $\tau \in \mathcal{T}$ is the $\tau$-quantile $\inf\{v : \hat F(v) \ge \tau\}$ of this 122-point discrete distribution $\hat F$.

### Bandwidth selection by leave-one-season-out log score

The parameters $\theta = (\log h_1, \dots, \log h_7, \log\lambda)$ are chosen to maximize the leave-one-season-out log score of the **timing class** on a tuning set $\mathcal{Q}$ of training rows:
$$
\hat\theta = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta}\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{Q}} \log\Bigl[(1 - \eta)\, \bar\pi^{\text{A}, -s(i)}_{k^+_i}(\phi_i; \theta) + \eta\, \bar\pi^{\text{base}}_{k^+_i}(\phi_i) + 10^{-12}\Bigr].
$$
Here $\bar\pi^{\text{A}, -s(i)}$ is the analog timing distribution for row $i$ computed with every row of $i$'s calendar season $s(i)$ (all sources and locations) removed from its analogs; both components are restricted to the allowed classes at $t_i$ and renormalized (if all analog weights vanish, the analog part is uniform over the allowed classes). The source discount is capped at 1 by using $\lambda = \exp\{\min(\theta_8, 0)\}$. As explained in @sec-loso, leaving out whole seasons is essential: otherwise the best analog for every row is its own season one week earlier, and the chosen bandwidths collapse toward zero. The size part does not enter the objective; it uses the bandwidths chosen for timing.

**Strengths and weaknesses.** KCDE has few parameters, its timing and size come from the same analogs, and it works well when the current season resembles past ones. It is methodologically very different from GBQR, which is why the two are both designated. Its main weakness is seasons without good analogs; the mixture weight $\eta$ addresses the worst consequences.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**KCDE settings** (`kcde.py`, `PeakKCDEModelConfig`).

- Analog window: `sw_radius = 4` season weeks.
- Mixture weight: $\eta$ = `baseline_mix` = 0.05, for both timing and size.
- Tuning set: `num_tuning_rows` = 2000 rows drawn without replacement with a fixed seed, up to half of them NHSN rows and the rest ILINet and FluSurv-NET rows.
- Optimizer: Nelder–Mead (`scipy.optimize.minimize`) from $h_\iota = 0.5$ for all $\iota$ and $\lambda = 0.5$, with an initial simplex of unit steps on the log scale ($\theta_0$ and $\theta_0 + e_\iota$ for each coordinate direction $e_\iota$), at most `max_tuning_iter` = 200 iterations (10 with `--short_run`), `xatol = 1e-2`, `fatol = 1e-4`.
- The fitted bandwidths on the original feature scales, $h_\iota\,\mathrm{sd}_\iota$, are stored as `bandwidths_`, and the tuning log score as `tuning_score_`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternatives considered"}
A state vector containing the recent trajectory shape $\bigl(\log\{(x_{t-n} + \varepsilon)/(M_t + \varepsilon)\}\bigr)_{n = 0, \dots, 3}$ and $\log(1 + d_t)$; kernel smoothing of the size distribution in $z$ with an outcome bandwidth; a joint timing-and-size LOSO objective; L-BFGS optimization from a rule-of-thumb start; joint $(k, z)$ draws for the backfill simulation; and a warning when the **effective number of analogs**, $n_{\text{eff}} = 1 / \sum_i \varpi_i^2$, is small. None of these is implemented, although $n_{\text{eff}}$ remains a useful diagnostic.
:::

## Model 4: Bayesian hierarchical model of timing and size (`peak_hier`) {#sec-hier}

::: {.callout-warning title="Status: evaluated on development seasons only"}
The model is implemented in `idmodels/peak/hier.py` (idmodels commit 8c56bf0). It has been fit with full MCMC settings and scored on the two ILINet development seasons (@sec-dev-results). It has **not** yet been run on the NHSN test seasons. Development results favor a weaker likelihood tempering than the committed default (@sec-hier-temper); the default has not been changed pending a decision.
:::

### In plain terms

GBQR and KCDE each learn one rule, shared by every location and season, that maps "what the season looks like now" to "when and how high the peak will be". The hierarchical model uses the same kind of rule. It adds two adjustments that the others lack:

- a **season adjustment**, shared by every state in the season (some seasons peak early everywhere, others late); and
- a **location adjustment**, shared by every season of a state (some states tend to peak earlier than others).

What makes the season adjustment useful in real time is that the model *learns the current season's adjustment from the current season*, using every state at once. Picture mid-January with 45 states observed. Suppose 30 of them have been rising for six weeks without peaking. Then the historical rule, which would have expected many of them to have peaked by now, is too early for *this* season, so the season's timing adjustment moves toward "later". Every state's forecast then shifts later, including the 15 states whose own data say little yet. That is the "pooling across locations" the other models do not have. The development results show that it matters: without it, forecasts made 5 to 8 weeks before the peak are much worse (@sec-dev-results).

The model has three parts, each with its own season (and, for timing, location) adjustment:

1. **Has the peak already happened?** A probability, given the current state of the season.
2. **If not, when?** For each future week, the chance that the peak comes that week, given that it has not come earlier (a "hazard", as in survival analysis).
3. **How big?** Given how many weeks away the peak is, the distribution of the remaining growth $z$.

Parts 2 and 3 are linked: a peak eight weeks away is expected to be much higher, relative to today, than one next week. So the model gives joint forecasts of timing and size.

### What this model adds

The models so far treat two kinds of structure only indirectly.

1. **Seasons differ as a whole.** In some seasons almost every state peaks around Christmas; in others the peak comes in February or March, or a second virus produces a late wave. All locations in a season are exposed to the same viruses, so their peaks are correlated. When half the states have already peaked, that is informative about the other half. GBQR and KCDE see this only through the national and synchrony features.
2. **Locations differ persistently.** Some states tend to peak earlier than others, for example because of when school terms start, which strains arrive first, or the mix of urban and rural populations. The NHSN record for any one state is only two or three usable seasons long, far too short to estimate a state-specific tendency from NHSN alone, but the same state has eight or more seasons of ILINet data.

A **hierarchical** (multilevel) model represents both with random effects: a **season effect** shared by all locations and sources in a season, and a **location effect** shared by all seasons and sources for a location. The key feature for real-time use is that the *current* season's effect is estimated from the current season's data in every location at once (@sec-hier-current).

### Data and notation

The model is fit to the same season-replay rows as the other models (@sec-replay). Row $i$ comes from source $g_i$, location $l_i$ and season $s_i$, has current week $t_i$, standardized feature vector $\phi_i$ (below), and outcomes $k_i = W^* - t_i$ and $z_i$ (@sec-relative). For each row we also need the set of candidate peak offsets
$$
\mathcal{M}_i = \{m \ge 1 : t_i + m \in \mathcal{W}\},
$$
the offsets $m$ for which $t_i + m$ is a window week. Its largest element is $m^{\max}_i = \overline\omega - t_i$. When the window has not yet opened ($t_i < \underline\omega$), the smallest element is $\underline\omega - t_i$, not 1.

### Timing: "already peaked" plus a discrete-time hazard

Timing is modeled in two stages, which mirror how a person reads a season. First: has the peak already happened? Then, if not: when will it happen?

**Stage 1, already peaked.** Once the window has opened ($t_i \ge \underline\omega$), the probability that the running maximum is the season's peak ($k_i \le 0$) is
$$
\pi_{0,i} = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}\bigl(a_0(t_i) + \phi_i^\top \beta_0 + \gamma_{g_i,0} + r_{i,0}\bigr),
$$
where $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x})$ maps any real number to a probability. Here $a_0(t)$ is a smooth function of the current week, $\beta_0$ is a coefficient vector, $\gamma_{g,0}$ is a source effect and $r_{i,0}$ is the random effect defined below. Before the window opens, $\pi_{0,i} = 0$.

**Stage 2, when.** If the peak is still to come, it occurs at week $t_i + m$ for some $m \in \mathcal{M}_i$. We model this with a **discrete-time hazard**, the standard tool of survival analysis for event times measured in whole weeks. The hazard $\chi_{i,m}$ is the probability that the peak is at offset $m$, *given that it is not at any earlier offset in* $\mathcal{M}_i$:
$$
\operatorname{logit} \chi_{i,m} = f_\omega(t_i + m) + f_m(m) + \phi_i^\top \beta + (\log m - \bar c_m)\,\phi_i^\top \beta_m + \gamma_{g_i,1} + r_{i,1},
\qquad m \in \mathcal{M}_i,\ m < m^{\max}_i,
$$
and $\chi_{i,m^{\max}_i} = 1$, because the peak must fall in the window. Then
$$
\Pr(k_i = m \mid k_i \ge 1) = \chi_{i,m} \prod_{m' \in \mathcal{M}_i,\, m' < m} (1 - \chi_{i,m'}),
\qquad
\Pr(k^+_i = m) = (1 - \pi_{0,i}) \Pr(k_i = m \mid k_i \ge 1).
$$
The probabilities over $m \in \mathcal{M}_i$ sum to one automatically because the last hazard is 1.

The terms have these roles:

- $f_\omega(w)$, a smooth function of the calendar week $w$ of the candidate peak, captures seasonality: peaks are common in late December through February and rare in October or May.
- $f_m(m)$, a smooth function of $\log m$, captures how the chance of peaking depends on how far ahead we look.
- $\phi_i^\top\beta$ shifts the hazard according to the current state of the season. For example, fast recent growth makes a peak next week less likely.
- $(\log m - \bar c_m)\,\phi_i^\top \beta_m$ lets the effect of the state depend on the offset. For example, a falling series makes a peak in 1–2 weeks unlikely but says less about a second peak 10 weeks away. $\bar c_m$ is the mean of $\log m$ over the training rows' risk sets (the offsets at which a row's peak had not yet happened), so $\beta$ is the effect at a typical offset. Centering reduces the correlation between $\beta$ and $\beta_m$ in the posterior.

**In plain terms.** Think of walking forward week by week from today. At each future week the model asks: "given that the peak hasn't come yet, is this the week?" The answer depends on the calendar (January is peak season), on how far ahead we are looking, on what the season looks like now, and on the season and location adjustments. Multiplying "not this week" answers together gives the chance that the peak is still ahead at any week, which is what the censored update of @sec-hier-current uses.

**Why a hazard instead of a softmax over offsets?** A softmax needs a separate parameter per offset, and offsets far ahead are rare in the data. A hazard with smooth terms in $w$ and $m$ shares strength across offsets and handles the window boundary exactly. It is also the form that makes the censored observations of @sec-hier-current easy to write down.

### Size given timing

For rows whose peak is still ahead ($k_i \ge 1$), the remaining log growth $z_i > 0$ is modeled on the **square-root scale**, *conditional on the timing*:
$$
\sqrt{z_i} \sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(\mu_i, \sigma_i),
$$
$$
\mu_i = b(t_i) + b_1 (\log k_i - \bar c_k) + b_2 (\log k_i - \bar c_k)^2 + \phi_i^\top\beta_z + (\log k_i - \bar c_k)\,\phi_i^\top \beta_{zm} + \gamma_{g_i,2} + r_{i,2},
$$
$$
\log \sigma_i = c_0 + c_1 (\log k_i - \bar c_k) + c_2 (t_i - 24)/10 + c_{g_i}.
$$
Here $\mathcal{N}^{+}(\mu, \sigma)$ is a normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ truncated to $(0, \infty)$, $b(t)$ is a smooth function of the current week, and $\bar c_k$ is the mean of $\log k$ over the training rows with $k \ge 1$. If the peak has already occurred, $z = 0$ exactly (@sec-relative).

In words: given that the peak is $k$ weeks away, the square root of the remaining log growth is roughly normal, with a center and spread that depend on $k$, the current week, the state of the season and the random effects.

Some explanation of these choices:

- **Conditioning on $k$.** A peak that is eight weeks away will be much higher, relative to today, than one that is next week. With $\log k$ in the mean and in the scale, the model captures this directly. Timing and size then come from one joint distribution: a draw of the timing implies a distribution for the size, and anything that shifts the timing (such as the current season's effect) also shifts the size.
- **Why the square root?** Grouping the training rows (ILINet and FluSurv-NET before 2018/19) by $k$, we compared transformations of $z$:
    - $z$ itself is right-skewed (skewness 0.6–2.1 across $k$ groups).
    - $\log z$ over-corrects and is strongly *left*-skewed (skewness −0.8 to −2.3), because peaks only slightly above the current maximum give very negative $\log z$.
    - $\sqrt{z}$ is close to symmetric (skewness −0.2 to 0.5) with near-normal tails (excess kurtosis −0.4 to 0.6) in every $k$ group.

  A first version of the model used a Student-$t$ distribution for $\log z$. Its fitted degrees of freedom went to about 1 (Cauchy-like tails), because it was trying to fit that long left tail, and the resulting posterior was hard to sample. The $\log$-$t$ version remains available as an option (`size_scale = "log"`).
- **Truncation at zero** keeps $z > 0$ for rows before the peak. Rows before the window opens can in principle have $z \le 0$ (@sec-relative), and those have $\sqrt{\max(z, 0)} = 0$. This is a slight approximation that affects very few rows.
- **Draws are capped** at the largest $z$ seen in training plus 1 (a growth factor of about 2.7 beyond the most extreme training row), as a guard against implausible upper quantiles.

### Random effects and partial pooling

The random effect of row $i$ has three components, one each for the already-peaked probability, the hazard and the size:
$$
r_i = u_{l_i} + v_{s_i} \in \mathbb{R}^3, \qquad
u_l \sim \mathcal{N}_3(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma_{\text{loc}}), \qquad
v_s \sim \mathcal{N}_3(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma_{\text{sea}}),
$$
independently across locations and seasons.

- **Location effect** $u_l$. Shared by all sources with the same location code. NHSN, ILINet and FluSurv-NET all use two-digit FIPS codes for states and "US" for the nation, so Massachusetts' eight ILINet seasons inform its NHSN forecasts. HHS regions appear only in ILINet and get their own effects.
- **Season effect** $v_s$. Shared by all locations *and all sources* in a calendar season, since they observe the same epidemic.
- **Components and correlation.** By default the three components are **independent** ($\Sigma$ diagonal, with SDs $\tau \in \mathbb{R}^3_+$), and the **location effect has only a hazard component** (@sec-hier-compute explains both choices). An optional version with LKJ-correlated components, $\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\tau)\,\Omega\,\operatorname{diag}(\tau)$, would let late seasons also tend to be large. It would also let timing information about the current season update its size forecast through the correlation. However, the correlations were too poorly identified to sample. Without them, the current season's timing still affects its size forecast through the model for size given $k$, but its size component $v_{s_0,2}$ is informed only by the censored size bounds.

To see how partial pooling works, consider the simplest case: $n_l$ independent observations for location $l$ with mean $\bar z_l$, observation variance $\sigma^2$, and a location effect $u_l \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$. The posterior mean of the effect is $B_l(\bar z_l - \mu)$ with $B_l = (n_l/\sigma^2)/(n_l/\sigma^2 + 1/\tau^2)$. It follows the location's own data when $n_l$ is large and shrinks toward the common mean when $n_l$ is small, and $\tau$ itself is estimated from the data.

**Source effects.** $\gamma_g \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and the scale offsets $c_g$ are fixed effects, with ILINet as the reference source ($\gamma_{\text{ILINet}} = 0$, $c_{\text{ILINet}} = 0$), since ILINet contributes the most rows. They let NHSN (or NSSP) differ systematically from ILINet. With only two or three NHSN seasons they are estimated imprecisely, and the posterior carries that uncertainty into the forecast.

### Tempering: rows of a series are not independent {#sec-hier-temper}

A likelihood that multiplies over replay rows treats every row as an independent observation. As @sec-loso explains, the roughly 39 rows of one (source, location, season) series all describe the same peak: $k$ decreases by exactly one from each row to the next, and $z$ changes little. An untempered posterior would therefore behave as if it had about 39 times more evidence than it does. Its intervals would be far too narrow, and the random-effect variances, which compare between-series with within-series variation, would be distorted.

We use a **tempered** (power) likelihood: every row's log likelihood is multiplied by a weight $w_{\text{lik}} \in (0, 1]$,
$$
\log p(\theta \mid \text{data}) = \text{const} + \log p(\theta) + w_{\text{lik}} \sum_i \bigl[\ell^{\text{timing}}_i(\theta) + \mathbf{1}\{k_i \ge 1\}\,\ell^{\text{size}}_i(\theta)\bigr],
$$
where $\theta$ denotes all parameters, $\ell^{\text{timing}}_i = \log \pi_{0,i}$ if $k_i \le 0$ and $\log \Pr(k^+_i = k_i)$ otherwise, and $\ell^{\text{size}}_i$ is the log density of $\sqrt{z_i}$. With $w_{\text{lik}} = 0.15$ each series counts as about six observations. This is a pragmatic device, not a model of the dependence (a series-level effect would be the more complete alternative). Its value mainly affects the width of the parameter posterior and the strength of the current-season update.

**In plain terms.** The weight says how many independent observations one season of one state is worth. At 0.15 it is worth about six, at 0.05 about two, and at 0.02 less than one. A smaller weight makes the model less sure of its fitted rule and its random-effect sizes, so the prior and the current-season evidence count for relatively more.

**What development showed.** Weaker tempering was better in both development seasons, and more so with each step down: log score −1.76 at 0.15, −1.68 at 0.05, and −1.66 at 0.02 (with the current-season update restricted to the hazard and size components, which on its own made no difference). The gain is largest in the weeks around the peak (@sec-dev-results). The committed default is still `likelihood_weight = 0.15`. Changing it to 0.02, and testing still smaller values, is pending a decision.

When origins are thinned (`origin_stride` $= 3$, every third origin week), each row's weight is multiplied by 3, so every series keeps the same total weight. Neighboring origins are near-duplicates, so little information is lost.

### Priors

All features are standardized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 in the training rows and clipped to $\pm 5$. They are then **whitened**: rotated and rescaled, using the eigendecomposition of their training covariance, into uncorrelated combinations with unit variance. The features are strongly collinear. For example, `rel_max`, `rm3` and `cum_rel` all measure the current level relative to the maximum. Without whitening the coefficients are highly correlated in the posterior, which makes sampling slow (@sec-hier-compute). Whitening changes the parameterization but not the model's fitted values, apart from the priors, which now apply to the uncorrelated combinations.

- Smooth functions $a_0$, $f_\omega$, $f_m$, $b$: cubic B-splines (6, 8, 5 and 6 basis functions, equally spaced knots) with $\mathcal{N}(0, 2^2)$ priors on the coefficients. $f_m$ drops its first basis function so that it has no intercept of its own.
- Coefficients: $\beta_0, \beta, \beta_z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ elementwise; the offset interactions $\beta_m, \beta_{zm} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5^2)$; $b_1, b_2, c_0, c_1, c_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$; source effects $\gamma_g \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $c_g \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5^2)$.
- Random effects: SDs $\tau \sim \text{Half-Normal}(0.5)$ elementwise (Gelman 2006), for the active components only (the hazard component for locations; all three for seasons). The effects are **centered** ($u_l \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$ directly), which samples well when each group has a lot of data, except the season effect of the already-peaked component, which is **non-centered** ($v_{s,0} = \tau_0 \tilde v_{s,0}$, $\tilde v_{s,0} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$) because its SD has posterior mass near zero (@sec-hier-compute).
- With the optional LKJ-correlated effects (`correlated_effects = True`, not used), the Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix has an LKJ(2) prior (Lewandowski, Kurowicka and Joe 2009). With the optional log-scale size model (`size_scale = "log"`, not used), $\nu - 1 \sim \text{Gamma}(2, 0.1)$.

On the logit scale a standard deviation of 0.5 corresponds to shifting a hazard of 0.2 to roughly 0.13–0.29, a moderate between-season or between-location difference. The fitted SDs were larger for the season effect on the hazard (posterior median about 1.5) and smaller for the location effect on the hazard (about 0.6).

### Computation {#sec-hier-compute}

The posterior is sampled with NUTS. The first version sampled very slowly: every iteration used the maximum of 255 leapfrog steps, with step sizes around 0.002. Finding out why took several steps, and they are recorded here because the reasons say something about the model.

1. **Collinear features and an ill-suited size scale.** At the posterior mode, the curvature (eigenvalues of the Hessian of the log posterior) spanned a factor of about $10^6$. Whitening the features, centering $\log k$ and $\log m$, and switching to the $\sqrt{z}$ size model (which removes the badly identified $\nu$) reduced this, but not enough on their own.
2. **The random-effect covariance was the real problem.** Starting from the mode and perturbing one block of parameters at a time, every block of fixed effects behaved like a Gaussian. The random-effect parameters did not.
    - **Non-centered season effects** (effects written as SD × standard normal) gave a long curved ridge between each season-effect SD and the standardized effects. This is the known failure of that parameterization when each group has a lot of data, and every season has hundreds of series.
    - **Centered effects** removed the ridge, but the **LKJ correlations** among the three effect components were pushed toward $\pm 1$. They are barely identified from about 20 seasons.
3. **What works.** The implementation now uses:
    - **independent** effect components (no estimated correlations);
    - **centered** effects, except that the season effect of the already-peaked component is non-centered, because its SD has posterior mass near zero, where the centered form has a funnel;
    - **location effects on the hazard only.** In the development fit, the location SDs for the already-peaked and size components were essentially zero (about 0.05 and 0.008 on their scales), against about 0.6 for the hazard. Locations differ in *when* they peak, not in the other two respects.
    - **thinned origins:** every third origin week (`origin_stride = 3`), with each row's likelihood weight multiplied by 3, so every series keeps the same total weight. Neighboring origins are near-duplicates, so little information is lost.

With these choices, on the 2018/19 development fit, no iteration reached the step limit (mean 64 leapfrog steps). All parameters had effective sample sizes of 15–160 from 200 draws of a single chain, and 500 iterations took about 4.5 minutes.

Things that did *not* help in a benchmark: a dense mass matrix adapted during warm-up; starting at the mode; and using the inverse Hessian at the mode as a fixed metric (a Laplace preconditioner). The last two fail because the joint mode of a hierarchical model is degenerate in the effect SDs. They remain available as options.

### Learning the current season's effect from censored observations {#sec-hier-current}

When forecasting season $s_0$, the training data contain no rows from $s_0$, so without further steps its season effect $v_{s_0}$ would simply be a draw from $\mathcal{N}_3(0, \Sigma_{\text{sea}})$. But the current season has already revealed something in every location. Suppose location $l$ is observed through week $t$ with running maximum $M_t$ reached at week $A_t$. Ignoring revisions, two facts are certain (@sec-relative, "What these targets look like when the data are final"):

- the peak is no earlier than $A_t$: $W^* \ge A_t$; and
- the peak is no lower than $M_t$: $Y^* \ge M_t$.

Now look back at any earlier origin $t' < A_t$ of the current season. Its outcomes $(k_{t'}, z_{t'})$ are not known yet, but they are **right-censored**: we know lower bounds for them,
$$
k_{t'} \ge \kappa_{t'} := A_t - t' \;(\ge 1), \qquad z_{t'} \ge \zeta_{t'} := \log(M_t + \varepsilon) - \log(M_{t'} + \varepsilon).
$$
The features $\phi_{t'}$ at that origin are computed from data through $t'$ only, exactly as for a training row. Under the model, the probability of what we know is
$$
\Pr(k_{t'} \ge \kappa_{t'},\, z_{t'} \ge \zeta_{t'})
= (1 - \pi_{0,t'}) \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}_{t'},\, m \ge \kappa_{t'}} \Pr(k_{t'} = m \mid k_{t'} \ge 1)\; \Pr\bigl(z_{t'} \ge \zeta_{t'} \mid k_{t'} = m\bigr),
$$
where the size factor is omitted (set to 1) when $\zeta_{t'} \le z_{\min}$. Each such term involves $v_{s_0}$. Collecting them over all locations and all origins $t' < A_t$ gives a likelihood for the current season's effect. For example, if many locations have been rising for weeks without peaking, these terms push the hazard component of $v_{s_0}$ down (a later season). If many have already reached high levels relative to their early-season values, the size component moves up.

**Computation.** Refitting the whole model by MCMC at every reference date would be slow, so the current-season effect is updated separately. For each posterior draw $\theta^{(d)}$ of the other parameters (from the fit to training seasons), we

1. find the mode $\hat v^{(d)}$ of the conditional log posterior of $v_{s_0}$,
$$
w_{\text{lik}} \sum_{l,\, t' < A_{l,t}} \log \Pr\bigl(k_{l,t'} \ge \kappa_{l,t'},\, z_{l,t'} \ge \zeta_{l,t'} \mid \theta^{(d)}, v_{s_0}\bigr) - \tfrac12 v_{s_0}^\top \bigl(\Sigma_{\text{sea}}^{(d)}\bigr)^{-1} v_{s_0},
$$
by damped Newton steps (12 iterations; the step length is capped at 1);
2. draw $v^{(d)}_{s_0} \sim \mathcal{N}_3\bigl(\hat v^{(d)}, H^{(d)-1}\bigr)$, where $H^{(d)}$ is the negative Hessian at the mode (a **Laplace approximation**).

The same tempering weight is applied, so that each location's censored rows count as a few observations, not dozens. The censored rows use every origin week (no thinning), with weight $w_{\text{lik}}$ per row, or a separate weight set by `current_update_weight` (@sec-hier-hybrid).

**A worked illustration.** Take mid-January of a season in which peaks come late. Of 45 states, 30 have been rising steadily for six weeks, with their running maximum set in the current week. For each of those states and each earlier origin $t'$ (say the six origins from mid-December on) we know the peak is at least $A_t - t'$ weeks after $t'$, that is, it had not happened by then. That gives $30 \times 6 = 180$ censored rows, each saying "the peak was still ahead". The historical rule, fitted to other seasons, would have given many of those rows a sizeable probability of peaking within a few weeks. Each row's likelihood term is therefore larger when the hazard is lower, and together they pull the hazard component of $v_{s_0}$ down, toward a later season. With $w_{\text{lik}} = 0.15$ the 180 rows count as about 27 observations, enough to move $v_{s_0}$ by a sizeable fraction of its prior SD. The shift then applies to every state, including those whose own data are not yet informative. The size bounds work the same way: if those states are already far above their mid-December levels, the size component moves up.

**Restricting the update.** One might worry that this evidence is lopsided for the already-peaked component. Every censored row says "not yet peaked at $t'$", which pushes the already-peaked probability down for the whole season, including at the current week. The option `current_update_components = [1, 2]` updates only the hazard and size components (the already-peaked component keeps its prior draw). In development it made no difference (@sec-dev-results), so the default updates all three. Location effects of the current locations are held at their posterior draws (or drawn from $\mathcal{N}_3(0, \Sigma_{\text{loc}}^{(d)})$ for a location not seen in training) and are not updated by the current season.

Two approximations should be kept in mind. First, the conditional posterior of $v_{s_0}$ given $\theta^{(d)}$ is approximated by a normal distribution. It has only three dimensions and draws on hundreds of censored terms, so this should be accurate. Second, $\theta$ is not updated by the current season, which ignores a small amount of information. For NHSN the bounds use the currently reported values, which can still be revised. A downward revision of the current maximum could in principle make a bound slightly wrong, but the effect on a season-level parameter estimated from many locations is small.

### Prediction

For a current-season series with features $\phi$ at week $t$, and each of $D = 200$ posterior draws $d$ (with its own $v^{(d)}_{s_0}$ and $u^{(d)}_l$):

- **Timing:** compute $\pi_0$ and the class probabilities $\Pr(k^+ = m)$ for $m \in \mathcal{M}$ from the formulas above. The model's timing output is the average over draws.
- **Size:** draw five joint samples $(k^+, z)$: $k^+$ from the class probabilities, then $z = 0$ if $k^+ = 0$ and otherwise $\sqrt{z} \sim \mathcal{N}^{+}(\mu, \sigma)$ evaluated at $k = k^+$ (drawn by inverting the truncated normal CDF). The model's size output is the set of quantiles of the resulting 1,000 values of $z$.

These outputs then pass through the same backfill simulation, floor and formatting as the other models (@sec-backfill, @sec-submission).

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**`PeakHierModel`** (`idmodels/peak/hier.py`; configuration `PeakHierModelConfig`).

- **Features** (`design_features`): `rel_max`, `log1p(min(wks_since_max, 15))`, `g1`, `g3`, `rm3`, `cum_rel`, `hist_rel` (0 if missing) and an indicator that it is missing, `nat_rel_max`, `log1p(min(nat_wks_since_max, 15))`, `nat_g3` (each replaced by the series' own value if there is no national series) and an indicator of that. `season_week` enters only through the splines; `g2` is not used. All 12 are standardized with the training mean and SD (a column with no variation keeps SD 1), clipped to $\pm 5$, and whitened (`whiten_features = True`; directions with near-zero variance are dropped). $\log k$ and $\log m$ are centered at their training means (over size rows and over hazard risk-set entries).
- **Splines**: `df_t = 6` (for $a_0$ and $b$, knots over season weeks `replay_start_week`..`window_end_week`), `df_week = 8` ($f_\omega$, over the window), `df_offset = 5` ($f_m$, over $\log m \in [0, \log 42]$).
- **Likelihood**: `likelihood_weight` $= w_{\text{lik}} = 0.15$ per replay row (multiplied by `origin_stride` when origins are thinned); `size_scale = "sqrt"` (the alternative `"log"` uses a Student-$t$ for $\log\max(z, z_{\min})$ if `student_t = True`, with `z_floor` $= z_{\min} = 0.01$); `origin_stride = 3` (every third origin week).
- **Effects**: `location_effects = True` with `location_components = [1]` (hazard only), `season_effects = True` with `season_components = [0, 1, 2]`, `correlated_effects = False`, `centered_effects = True` except `season_noncentered_components = [0]`, `effect_scale = 0.5` (Half-Normal scale of $\tau$), `current_season_update = True`.
- **MCMC**: NUTS (NumPyro; Phan, Pradhan and Jankowiak 2019) with `num_chains = 2` chains run sequentially, `num_warmup = 500`, `num_samples = 500`, `target_accept_prob = 0.85`, `max_tree_depth = 8`; `whiten_features = True`; diagonal mass matrix adapted during warm-up. (Options not used by default: `dense_mass`, `init_map_steps`, `laplace_mass`.) The condition number of $H$ is stored as `laplace_condition_`, and timings and step statistics as `mcmc_stats_`. Diagnostics stored after fitting: `max_rhat_`, `min_ess_` (over all parameters except the individual effects $u_l$, $v_s$) and `num_divergences_`. The fit is repeated once per forecast season, as for the other models.
- **Prediction**: `num_posterior_draws = 200` (evenly spaced over the retained draws), `size_samples_per_draw = 5`, `laplace_iters = 12`. The current-season update and prediction are deterministic given the reference date (seeded random numbers).
- **Options explored in development, off by default** (@sec-dev-results): `time_varying_coefs` (feature effects on the already-peaked probability and the hazard vary linearly with the current week); `wsm_dummies` (indicators for 0, 1, 2 and 3 weeks since the maximum); `current_update_components` (which components the censored update informs; default `[0, 1, 2]`); `sync_burden_features` (the synchrony and burden features of @sec-features); `correlated_effects` (LKJ-correlated components); `size_scale = "log"` (Student-$t$ for $\log z$); and the sampler options `dense_mass`, `init_map_steps` and `laplace_mass` (MAP start with the inverse Hessian as a fixed metric). The last three did not improve sampling.
- **Timing**: a full fit (2 chains × 1,000 iterations, `origin_stride = 3`) takes about 20 minutes per season on an 8-core laptop without contention. In the development runs: mean 63–95 leapfrog steps, no divergences, largest $\hat R$ 1.03–1.10, smallest effective sample size 35–108.
- **Hook**: the current-season update runs in `PeakHierModel._observe_current_season`, which the base class calls with the current season as reported (`CurrentSeason`) just before `_predict`.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Decisions and open questions"}
Decided or learned in development (@sec-dev-results):

1. **Tempering.** $w_{\text{lik}} = 0.15$ was too strong. Values of 0.05 and 0.02 scored better in both development seasons, with 0.02 best. The committed default is still 0.15, pending a decision. Values below 0.02 have not been tried.
2. **Effect structure.** Correlated (LKJ) effect components were dropped: the correlations could not be sampled. Location effects are on the hazard only. Effects are centered, except the season effect of the already-peaked component.
3. **Size model.** $\sqrt{z}$ given $k$, a truncated normal, replaced $\log z$ with a Student-$t$.
4. **The current-season update helps.** Without it (`current_season_update = False`), log scores 5 to 8 weeks before the peak dropped from −2.3 to −3.2.
5. **What did not help:** time-varying coefficients; indicators for weeks since the maximum; restricting the current-season update to the hazard and size components; and the synchrony and burden features.

Still open:

6. **Weakness around the peak.** Every `peak_hier` variant is weaker than `peak_gbqr` in the weeks around the peak: log score about −2.1 to −2.8, against −1.9 for `peak_gbqr`, one week either side of the peak. The first explanation was the model family: a logit-linear hazard might not separate "the peak is this week" from "next week" as sharply as trees. The hybrid (@sec-hier-hybrid) makes that unlikely. It takes GBQR's timing as an offset and still has the weakness (−2.54 against −1.97 in 2018/19).
   The evidence instead points to the censored current-season update being too strong:
   - `hier__nocur` has no weakness at the peak but is much worse earlier;
   - weaker tempering, which also weakens the update, narrows the gap;
   - `hybrid__w02` narrows it most (−2.15).

   The `current_update_weight` option tempers the update separately from training (`hybrid__cu01`, `hybrid__cu003`; not yet evaluated, @sec-future).
7. **Location and season effects shared across sources.** This assumes a state's tendency to peak early or late carries over from ILINet to NHSN, and that sources share a season effect. It is untested on NHSN.
8. **What the model does not have.** No series-level effect, no effects of virus type or subtype, and no dependence between the current-season effect and features beyond the national ones.
:::

### Hybrid: GBQR offsets (`peak_hybrid`) {#sec-hier-hybrid}

::: {.callout-warning title="Status: paused, partly evaluated"}
Implemented in `idmodels/peak/hybrid.py` (`PeakHybridModel`, `PeakHybridModelConfig`; idmodels 1dd468d) and `src/peak_hybrid`. It has been scored on the 2018/19 development season only; the remaining runs are on hold (@sec-future).
:::

**In plain terms.** The hierarchical model is better well before the peak, because it learns the current season's timing from all locations; GBQR is better around and after the peak, because its trees capture sharp combinations of the level, growth and weeks since the maximum (@sec-dev-results).

The hybrid is a single model that uses GBQR's forecasts as a starting point, or **offset**, for each part of the hierarchical model:

- GBQR's probability that the peak has already happened starts the already-peaked part;
- its implied weekly chances of peaking start the hazard;
- its median remaining growth starts the size part.

The hierarchical model then learns how far to trust GBQR, and adds what GBQR lacks: season and location adjustments, including the update of the current season's effect from censored observations. Unlike the equal-weight ensemble, how much weight goes to GBQR is estimated from the data.

**Offsets.** For each row, with GBQR's timing-class probabilities $\pi^{\text{G}}_0, \pi^{\text{G}}_1, \dots$ and quantiles $q^{\text{G}}(\tau)$ of $z$:
$$
o_0 = \operatorname{logit} \pi^{\text{G}}_0, \qquad
o_{m} = \operatorname{logit}\frac{\pi^{\text{G}}_m}{\sum_{m' \ge m,\, m' \in \mathcal{M}} \pi^{\text{G}}_{m'}} \;\; (m \in \mathcal{M}), \qquad
o_z = \sqrt{q^{\text{G}}\bigl(\pi^{\text{G}}_0 + (1 - \pi^{\text{G}}_0)/2\bigr)} .
$$
Here $o_m$ is the hazard implied by GBQR's class probabilities over the valid future offsets, and $o_z$ is the square root of GBQR's median of $z$ given that the peak is still to come. These enter the already-peaked logit, the hazard logits and the mean of $\sqrt{z}$ as $c_0 o_0$, $c_1 o_m$ and $c_2 o_z$, with coefficients $c_j \sim \mathcal{N}(1, 0.5^2)$. By default the hierarchical model's own linear feature terms are dropped (`hybrid_keep_features = False`), since GBQR already uses the features. What remains is the splines, source effects, location and season effects and the current-season update.

**Honest offsets for training.** If the training rows' offsets were GBQR's in-sample predictions, GBQR would look far more accurate than it is, and the hybrid would learn to trust it too much. Each of GBQR's bags leaves out about 30% of the training seasons, so every training row is given the **out-of-bag** prediction: the average over the bags that never saw the row's season (`PeakGBQRModel.oob_predict`). At forecast time all bags are used.

**Results so far** (2018/19 only, `@rtrev`, states). Log score: `hybrid__w02` −1.836 (the best single model that season, ahead of `ens_gbqr_hierw05` −1.849), `hybrid__feat` −1.855, `hybrid` −1.878, against `peak_gbqr` −1.867, `peak_baseline` −1.871 and `hier__w05` −1.927; relative log-WIS 0.64–0.67 for the hybrids against 0.695 for `peak_gbqr`. The GBQR offsets make the posterior better behaved (`hybrid`: largest $\hat R$ 1.01, smallest effective sample size 218), but `hybrid__w02` mixed poorly ($\hat R$ 1.29, effective sample size 12) and needs a longer run. The weakness around the peak remains (log score one week either side of the peak: `hybrid` −2.54, `hybrid__w02` −2.15, `peak_gbqr` −1.97), which is the evidence that the censored update is too strong and the reason for `current_update_weight` (@sec-hier-current).

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**`PeakHybridModel`** (`idmodels/peak/hybrid.py`, subclass of `PeakHierModel`; configuration `PeakHybridModelConfig`).

- **Settings.** `likelihood_weight = 0.05`, `offset_prior_sd = 0.5`, `hybrid_keep_features = False`; all other settings as `PeakHierModelConfig`.
- **Internal GBQR.** `gbqr_num_bags = 25`, `gbqr_bag_frac_samples = 0.7`, `gbqr_max_k = 12`, `gbqr_n_estimators = 100`, `gbqr_learning_rate = 0.05`, `gbqr_min_child_samples = 50`, using the same feature set as the hybrid's `sync_burden_features`. It is fit on every origin; the hierarchical part then thins origins as usual.
- **Offsets.** Probabilities are clipped to $[10^{-4}, 1 - 10^{-4}]$ before taking logits. Before the window opens, $\pi^{\text{G}}_0$ is set to 0 (so $o_0$ is irrelevant there). The offsets for the censored current-season rows are computed from GBQR predictions on those rows.
- **`current_update_weight`** (also available in `PeakHierModelConfig`): the likelihood weight of each censored current-season row, if different from `likelihood_weight`.
- **Cost.** About 40 minutes per season fit (GBQR plus MCMC) under the development machine's load, and GBQR predictions at every reference date.
:::

## Model 5: ensembles (`peak_ensemble`) {#sec-ensemble}

::: {.callout-warning title="Status: evaluated on development seasons only"}
Equal-weight ensembles of saved forecasts have been evaluated on the ILINet development seasons (`analysis/peak-models/ensemble_validation.py`; results in @sec-dev-results). There is no `peak_ensemble` model directory or hub submission yet, and no ensemble has been run on the NHSN test seasons.
:::

Combining forecasts from different models usually improves accuracy and robustness. Here there is also a specific reason: the hierarchical model and GBQR are good at different phases of the season (@sec-dev-results). The hierarchical model is better well before the peak, GBQR at and after it, so an average can be better than either. The two targets are combined differently, because they are different types of forecast.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the set of component models, indexed by $\mathfrak{m}$, with weights $\vartheta_{\mathfrak m} \ge 0$ and $\sum_{\mathfrak m \in \mathcal{M}} \vartheta_{\mathfrak m} = 1$.

**Peak week: linear pool.** For component pmfs $p^{\mathfrak m}$,
$$
p^{\text{ens}}(w) = \sum_{\mathfrak m \in \mathcal{M}} \vartheta_{\mathfrak m} \, p^{\mathfrak m}(w).
$$
The result is again a pmf, and if every component puts at least some value $\delta' > 0$ on every week, then so does the pool. A linear pool of calibrated but different forecasts tends to be somewhat too wide (Ranjan and Gneiting 2010); if the components are overconfident, as flexible models fitted to few seasons can be, this is not necessarily a disadvantage.

**Peak size: quantile averaging.** For component quantiles $q^{\mathfrak m}(\tau)$,
$$
q^{\text{ens}}(\tau) = \sum_{\mathfrak m \in \mathcal{M}} \vartheta_{\mathfrak m} \, q^{\mathfrak m}(\tau).
$$
This is also called **Vincentization**. An average of nondecreasing functions of $\tau$ is nondecreasing, so the result is a valid set of quantiles. Compared with pooling the distributions, quantile averaging keeps the typical spread of the components rather than widening it (Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne and Winkler 2013). This matches the behavior of `hubEnsembles::simple_ensemble()`, used by the `flu_flusion` model, whose default aggregation is the mean: for pmf outputs it averages probabilities (a linear pool) and for quantile outputs it averages quantiles.

**In plain terms.** For the peak week, the ensemble's probability for each week is the average of the members' probabilities. For the peak size, the ensemble's 10% quantile is the average of the members' 10% quantiles, and likewise for every level.

**Development result.** `ens_gbqr_hierw05`, the equal-weight ensemble of `peak_gbqr` and `hier__w05`, was the best forecaster on the development seasons on RPS and peak-size WIS. It beat both members on log score and WIS in each season: overall log score −1.61 against −1.63 (GBQR) and −1.68 (hierarchical), RPS 0.88 and WIS 0.60 relative to the baseline, and 95% coverage 0.94 (@sec-dev-results). Adding the baseline as a third member gave a slightly better log score (−1.60) but clearly worse WIS (0.69).

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Development ensembles** (`analysis/peak-models/ensemble_validation.py`): equal weights; only forecasts (reference date, location) made by every member are combined; pmfs are averaged and renormalized, and quantiles averaged level by level. Members' pmfs are already floored (@sec-floor), so the average is too. A `peak_ensemble` model directory producing hub files (with quantile averages rounded to integers after averaging, @sec-submission) and learned weights are listed in @sec-future.
:::

# Backfill and the probabilities of past weeks {#sec-backfill}

## Why past weeks need positive probability

Suppose that at time $t$ the currently reported maximum is at week $A_t$, and another past week $w \ne A_t$ is currently reported slightly lower. Under final data it could not be the peak, but with revisions it might: if week $w$ is later revised upward (or week $A_t$ downward) enough that its final value exceeds that of every other window week, it becomes the peak. If a model gives such a week probability exactly zero and it does become the peak, the log score (@sec-eval) of that forecast is $\log 0 = -\infty$, and so is any average that includes it. A single such event would make a model's average log score infinitely bad. More importantly, putting zero on a possible outcome is simply a wrong statement of uncertainty.

All models therefore share one post-processing step (`PeakModel._predict_current_season`), which (1) estimates how NHSN counts are revised, (2) simulates plausible final versions of the current season and applies the model to each, and (3) applies a floor to every window week.

## The revision model: a block bootstrap of revision vectors {#sec-revision}

Revisions are measured on **counts**. For location $l$, a vintage $a$ and a lag $j$, let $w = t_l(a) - j$ and define the **log revision ratio**
$$
\rho_{l,a,j} = \log \frac{c^{(a^\dagger)}_{l,w} + 1}{c^{(a)}_{l,w} + 1},
$$
where $a^\dagger$ is the latest vintage with as-of date on or before the reference date $r$, which serves as "final". It is positive if the week was revised upward after lag $j$, and zero if it was not revised. The offset $1$ keeps the ratio finite for zero counts. For each (vintage, location) pair we record the **revision vector** $\boldsymbol\rho_{l,a} = (\rho_{l,a,0}, \dots, \rho_{l,a,J-1})$ over the $J$ most recent weeks of that release.

Revisions of different weeks in one release are dependent: for example, a batch of late hospital reports raises the whole recent tail of a series together. Instead of modeling this dependence, the implementation resamples **whole vectors**, a form of block bootstrap: a draw of the revisions of the current release is a randomly chosen historical revision vector, which automatically carries the lag profile and the within-release dependence. Small counts are revised proportionally more, so vectors are grouped into **strata** by the reported lag-0 count $c^{(a)}_{l, t_l(a)}$, and the current release of location $l$ draws from the stratum of its own lag-0 count.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Revision model** (`revision.RevisionModel`, `revision.load_nhsn_vintages`).

- **Vintages.** All NHSN vintages (HHS archive before 2024-11-15, NHSN afterwards) with as-of date $\le r$, loaded as counts (`NHSNDataSource(rates=False)`); a few snapshots with a different file schema are skipped.
- **Lags.** $J$ = `PeakModelConfig.revision_max_lag` = 10, lags $j = 0, \dots, 9$ relative to each vintage's latest week for that location. Weeks at lag 10 or more are treated as final.
- **Maturity.** Only vintages with as-of date at least $J$ weeks before $a^\dagger$ are used, so that every recorded week has had at least 10 weeks to mature. Vectors with any lag missing are dropped. Vectors from all times of year and all locations (including the US) are pooled.
- **Strata.** Lag-0 count $< 50$, $[50, 500)$, and $\ge 500$ (`strata_bounds = (50, 500)`). If a location's stratum has fewer than 30 vectors (`min_stratum_vectors`), all vectors are used.
- **Draws.** $S$ = `num_revision_draws` = 200 vectors per location, drawn with replacement.
- **Fallback.** If fewer than 200 vectors exist in total (`min_vectors`; this happens early in the 2023/24 hindcasts), the $\rho_j$ are drawn independently as $\mathcal{N}\bigl(0, (0.1/(1 + j))^2\bigr)$: a small, symmetric perturbation that decays with lag, so that past weeks still receive some probability.
- **Revised counts.** For lag $j$ (week $t - j$), $\tilde c^{(b)}_{t-j} = \max\{(c_{t-j} + 1)\exp(\rho^{(b)}_j) - 1,\; 0\}$, where $c$ is the currently reported count and $b = 1, \dots, S$ indexes draws. Weeks older than lag 9 are left unchanged.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternatives considered"}
A parametric model $\rho_{l,w,j} = \zeta_j \Delta_{l,a} + \xi_{l,w,j}$, with Student-$t$ errors $\xi$ whose center and scale depend on the lag, a scale factor decreasing in population size, and a release effect $\Delta_{l,a}$ shared by all weeks of a release, fitted by maximum likelihood with $J = 9$ lags and heavier weight on vintages of the current NHSN system. The block bootstrap was preferred because it captures the within-release dependence and the lag profile without distributional assumptions. Stratifying the bootstrap by time of season is a possible refinement.
:::

## Monte Carlo over plausible final seasons {#sec-mc}

The models were trained on final data (@sec-replay), so they estimate the conditional distribution of the targets given the features of a *final* series. The current season's recent values are not final. The law of total probability resolves this:
$$
\Pr(W^* = w \mid \mathcal{F}_t) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[\, \Pr(W^* = w \mid \text{final values through } t) \;\big|\; \mathcal{F}_t \bigr],
$$
and likewise for the distribution function of $C^*$. The inner probability is what a model estimates; the outer expectation, over the unknown final values of the recent weeks, is approximated by averaging over the $S$ revision draws of @sec-revision. For each location $l$ and each draw $b = 1, \dots, S$:

1. **Revised series.** Form the revised counts $\tilde c^{(b)}_u$ and rates $\tilde y^{(b)}_u = 10^5\, \tilde c^{(b)}_u / N_l$ for $u \le t$.
2. **Features and predictions.** Compute the features of @sec-features from $\tilde y^{(b)}$ (national features from the US series of the same draw $b$). This gives draw-specific values $\tilde M^{(b)}_t$, $\tilde A^{(b)}_t$ and $\tilde\ell^{M(b)}_t = \log(\tilde M^{(b)}_t + \varepsilon_{\text{NHSN}})$, and the model outputs $\pi^{(b)}_j$ and $\hat Q^{(b)}_z(\tau)$.
3. **Allowed classes.** Set the probabilities of disallowed classes (@sec-classes-to-pmf) to zero and renormalize; call the result $\tilde\pi^{(b)}_j$.
4. **Timing pmf of the draw.** Map classes to weeks: class $j \ge 1$ to week $t + j$, and class $0$ to the week of the draw's own running maximum,
$$
p^{(b)}(w) = \sum_{j \ge 1} \tilde\pi^{(b)}_j\, \mathbf{1}\{w = t + j\} + \tilde\pi^{(b)}_0\, \mathbf{1}\{w = \tilde A^{(b)}_t\}, \qquad w \in \mathcal{W}.
$$
5. **Size draws.** Take $n_u = 200$ stratified levels $u_i = (i + 0.5)/200$, $i = 0, \dots, 199$ (so $u_i \in \{0.0025, 0.0075, \dots, 0.9975\}$). Map each through the piecewise-linear interpolation of the sorted 23 predicted quantiles, $z^{(b)}_i = \hat Q^{(b)}_z(u_i)$ (constant beyond the extreme levels 0.01 and 0.99, which affects only the outer 1% of each tail). An earlier version used $n_u = 50$ levels spanning exactly 0.01 to 0.99; with little revision spread the pooled 0.025 and 0.975 quantiles then came out near the model's 0.03 and 0.97 quantiles, making the 95% interval too narrow. If $t \ge \underline\omega$, replace $z^{(b)}_i$ by $\max(z^{(b)}_i, 0)$: once a window week has been observed, the final peak cannot be below the final running maximum. Convert to counts:
$$
C^{(b)}_i = \frac{N_l}{10^5}\,\max\Bigl\{\exp\bigl(\tilde\ell^{M(b)}_t + z^{(b)}_i\bigr) - \varepsilon_{\text{NHSN}},\; 0\Bigr\}.
$$

The timing forecast before the floor is the average $\hat p(w) = S^{-1} \sum_b p^{(b)}(w)$. The size forecast is formed from the pooled $S \cdot n_u = 40{,}000$ values $\{C^{(b)}_i\}$: the empirical quantiles at the 23 levels, which are the quantiles of the *mixture* of the draw-specific predictive distributions (not an average of quantiles).

**How past weeks get probability.** The class-0 probability of each draw goes to that draw's running maximum week $\tilde A^{(b)}_t$. For a sharply peaked series, $\tilde A^{(b)}_t = A_t$ in nearly every draw, so the past probability ends up almost entirely on $A_t$. For a flat-topped series, where several weeks are close to the maximum, revisions change which week is largest, and the class-0 probability is shared among those weeks. No ad hoc rule for "near-maximum" weeks is needed. Revisions also change the features, so they move probability between past and future weeks: for example, if the latest week is revised upward in a draw, `rel_max` and `g1` increase and the model gives more probability to a future peak.

**How revisions affect the peak size.** The size forecast depends on the revisions through $\tilde M^{(b)}_t$ (the revised running maximum is the base to which the growth $e^{z}$ is applied) and through the features that determine $\hat Q^{(b)}_z$. In particular the lower bound $C^* \ge$ (final running maximum) is enforced draw by draw, so a plausible upward revision of the past raises the forecast.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Monte Carlo settings** (`PeakModel._predict_current_season`).

- $S$ = `num_revision_draws` = 200 draws per location; $n_u$ = `num_size_levels` = 200 stratified levels per draw.
- The random number generator is seeded with the reference date (seconds since the Unix epoch), so forecasts are reproducible.
- Current-season counts come from the most recent vintage $a^\dagger$; they are forward-filled for the features but not gap-interpolated as the training series are.
- Empirical quantiles use `numpy.quantile` (linear interpolation between order statistics).
- **Grid resolution.** Because each draw contributes one value per 2% of probability, the pooled 0.025 and 0.975 quantiles correspond, when revision variability is small, to the model's 0.03 and 0.97 quantiles, slightly narrowing the 95% interval. A finer grid would remove this.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternatives considered"}
An earlier design drew $(k, z)$ from the model once per simulated final season, declared the peak to be in the future only if the simulated future value exceeded the revised past maximum $R^{(b)}$, and set the size to $\max(R^{(b)}, \tilde Y^{(b)})$ with $n_{\text{sim}} = 10{,}000$ draws and linear tail extrapolation. It was replaced by the algorithm above, which applies the model to features of each simulated final series and so matches how the models were trained. A variant that uses the simulation only to split $\pi_0$ among past weeks, leaving future-week probabilities unchanged, was also considered.
:::

## The probability floor $\delta$ {#sec-floor}

Finally, every one of the 34 window weeks, past or future, receives at least a floor $\delta$, and the result is renormalized:
$$
p_t(w) = \frac{\max\{\hat p(w), \delta\}}{Z_\delta}, \qquad Z_\delta = \sum_{u \in \mathcal{W}} \max\{\hat p(u), \delta\}.
$$
Since $1 \le Z_\delta \le 1 + n_{\mathcal{W}}\delta$, two bounds follow.

- **Protection.** For every week, $p_t(w) \ge \delta / (1 + n_{\mathcal{W}}\delta)$, so the log score of any outcome is at least $\log \delta - \log(1 + n_{\mathcal{W}} \delta)$. With $\delta = 10^{-4}$ and $n_{\mathcal{W}} = 34$ this is about $-9.21$. This covers every surprise the model does not anticipate: weeks that were impossible under the revision draws, and seasons unlike any in the history.
- **Small cost.** For every week, $p_t(w) \ge \hat p(w)/Z_\delta \ge \hat p(w)/(1 + n_{\mathcal{W}}\delta)$, so the floor lowers the log score of any outcome by at most $\log(1 + n_{\mathcal{W}}\delta) \approx 0.0034$.

The trade-off is a tiny, bounded cost when the model is right against protection from an unbounded loss when it is wrong. The value of $\delta$ should be roughly the frequency with which outcomes that the model considers essentially impossible actually occur.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Floor.** $\delta$ = `PeakModelConfig.pmf_floor` = $10^{-4}$, applied after averaging over draws with the max-then-renormalize rule above.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternatives considered"}
The mixture $(1 - n_{\mathcal{W}}\delta)\hat p + \delta$ gives the same guarantee.
:::

## Revisions in other sources: ILINet {#sec-revision-ilinet}

**In plain terms.** Different surveillance systems revise their data differently. NHSN admission counts mostly go *up* after first release, as late hospital reports arrive. ILINet × percent positive can go *either way*: the share of visits for influenza-like illness shifts as more clinics report (the number of patient visits grows after first release), and the percent positive changes as more laboratory specimens are counted (the specimen count often roughly doubles). The block bootstrap of @sec-revision assumes no direction. It resamples whole historical revision vectors of the source being forecast, so it carries over to ILINet unchanged, apart from a few settings.

- **Data.** Delphi Epidata keeps every weekly ILINet release: state-level ILI from the 2017/18 season on, clinical-lab percent positive from October 2018 (`analysis/peak-models/epidata_ilinet.py`). The as-published series at each reference date is rebuilt from values at lags 0–9 weeks; older weeks are taken as final.
- **Size of revisions** (states, 2018/19–2019/20). At first release the product differs from its final value by a median of about 6–9% on the log scale, with a 90th percentile of 45–65%; by lag 4 the median is below 1%. Up and down revisions are both common, and positivity drives most of the large ones. In 7 of 16 state-seasons checked, the peak week of the first-release series differed from that of the final series.
- **Effect on forecasts.** Forecasting from provisional ILINet as if it were final lowered the baseline's log score from −1.50 to −1.83 and its 95% peak-size coverage from 0.94 to 0.79. With revision simulation these became −1.66 and 0.92 (@sec-dev-results).

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**ILINet revision model** (`validate_ilinet.py --revisions`; `epidata_ilinet.revision_vintages`; `RevisionModel(max_lag=10, strata_bounds=(), offset=0.01, fallback_sd=0.25)`).

- **Vintages known at the reference date only.** Revision vectors come from releases whose latest week is on or before the reference date. Each is measured against the latest value available *at the reference date* (at most lag 9), never against today's final value.
- **Offset** 0.01 in ILINet units in the log ratios (instead of the $+1$ used for counts). **No strata**: all locations are pooled.
- **Fallback.** Before about mid-December 2018 fewer than 200 complete revision vectors exist, since clinical-lab vintages start in October 2018. Until then, a symmetric perturbation with lag-0 SD 0.25, decaying as $1/(1 + j)$, is used. That value was chosen with knowledge of the measured revision sizes above.
- $S = 200$ draws per location, as for NHSN.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Possible extensions"}
- **Condition revisions on information available at release time.** The bootstrap treats a state's lag-0 value as a draw from all states' revision histories. For ILINet, the size of a positivity revision depends strongly on how many specimens have been reported so far. For NHSN, the analogue is how complete hospital reporting is. A regression of the log revision ratio on lag, specimen count (or number of reporting hospitals) and location, for example a quantile regression in the spirit of Tang et al. (2025), should give sharper, better-targeted revision draws.
- **Make the hierarchical model's censored update robust to revisions.** The bounds "the peak is no earlier and no lower than the current maximum" (@sec-hier-current) use the reported data. With ILINet's two-way revisions a reported maximum can later be revised down. Computing the bounds on revision draws, rather than on the reported series, would account for this.
- **Train on real-time features.** An alternative is to train the models on features computed from provisional data, with targets from final data. This needs long vintage histories (ILINet vintages exist only from 2017/18, NHSN from 2022), so it is not practical yet.
:::

## Checking the revision probabilities

The backtest should check that the revision probabilities are **calibrated**: across all forecasts, the total probability that was assigned to past non-maximal weeks should roughly match how often a past non-maximal week actually became the final peak. Because such events are rare, this check is coarse, and it should be reported with its (season-blocked) uncertainty. This check is not yet part of `score_peak_forecasts.py` (@sec-future).

# From model output to a submission {#sec-submission}

The final steps convert the Monte Carlo output to integer counts and write rows in the hub format.

**Peak-size quantiles.** The pooled count values of @sec-mc already lie on the count scale (rates were converted with the same $N_l$ that formed them). Writing $\hat Q_{C}(\tau)$ for their empirical $\tau$-quantile, the submitted value is
$$
q_t(\tau) = \max_{\tau' \in \mathcal{T},\, \tau' \le \tau} \operatorname{round}\bigl(\max\{\hat Q_{C}(\tau'), 0\}\bigr),
$$
that is, rounding to the nearest integer, truncation at zero, and a running maximum over increasing levels. Rounding is nondecreasing, so it preserves the order of the quantiles, although it can create ties between adjacent levels, which are allowed; the running maximum is a safeguard. No hard floor at the currently *reported* maximum is imposed; the lower bound comes from the revised running maximum of each draw.

**The peak-week pmf.** The pmf after @sec-floor has 34 entries, all in $[0, 1]$, summing to 1 up to floating-point error; it is written at full precision without rounding.

**Hub format.** Each location contributes 34 rows with `target = "peak week inc flu hosp"`, `output_type = "pmf"`, `output_type_id` equal to the window date (YYYY-MM-DD) and `value` equal to its probability; and 23 rows with `target = "peak inc flu hosp"`, `output_type = "quantile"`, `output_type_id` equal to the level $\tau$ and `value` equal to the integer count. For both targets `horizon` and `target_end_date` are `NA`, and `reference_date` is $r$. Files are named `{reference_date}-UMass-peak_{model}.csv`, and `PeakModel.run` refuses to write a file that contains missing values. They must pass the hub's validation checks (`hubValidations`).

# Evaluation {#sec-eval}

## Proper scoring rules

A **scoring rule** $S(F, y)$ assigns a number to a forecast distribution $F$ and the outcome $y$ that occurred. We use the negatively oriented convention (smaller is better) unless stated otherwise. A scoring rule is **proper** if, whenever the outcome truly follows a distribution $G$, reporting $G$ is optimal in expectation:
$$
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim G}\, S(G, y) \le \mathbb{E}_{y \sim G}\, S(F, y) \quad \text{for all } F,
$$
and **strictly proper** if equality holds only for $F = G$ (Gneiting and Raftery 2007). Proper scores reward honest forecasts: a forecaster cannot improve their expected score by reporting something other than what they believe. Good probabilistic forecasts are **calibrated** (predicted probabilities match observed frequencies) and, subject to that, **sharp** (concentrated) (Gneiting, Balabdaoui and Raftery 2007).

## Log score for the peak week

For a pmf $p$ and observed peak week $W^*$, the **logarithmic score** (Good 1952) is
$$
\mathrm{LogS}(p, W^*) = \log p(W^*),
$$
using the natural logarithm and reported in its positively oriented form (larger is better; its negative is the corresponding loss). It is strictly proper for categorical outcomes, and it is **local**: it depends only on the probability given to the week that happened, not on how the remaining probability was spread. It is also unbounded below, which is why the floor of @sec-floor is essential. Earlier FluSight challenges scored seasonal targets with a log score truncated at $-10$ and with a "multibin" variant that credits probability within $\pm 1$ week of the truth (McGowan et al. 2019; Reich et al. 2019); the multibin score is not proper (Bracher 2019). We report the probability placed within $\pm 1$ week of the true peak, $p(W^*-1) + p(W^*) + p(W^*+1)$ (with terms outside the window omitted), only as a descriptive summary, not as a score.

## Ranked probability score for the peak week

Because weeks are ordered, it is natural to reward forecasts that are close even if not exact. Order the window weeks $w_1 < \dots < w_{34}$, let $P_i = \sum_{i' \le i} p(w_{i'})$ be the forecast cumulative distribution, and let $i^*$ be the index of the observed peak week. The **ranked probability score** (Epstein 1969) is
$$
\mathrm{RPS}(p, W^*) = \sum_{i=1}^{34} \bigl(P_i - \mathbf{1}\{i \ge i^*\}\bigr)^2,
$$
where the 34th term is always zero. It is the discrete analog of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), it is strictly proper, and a forecast one week off is penalized less than one ten weeks off. Some authors divide by $n_{\mathcal{W}} - 1$; we use the unnormalized form, whose units are weeks.

## Weighted interval score for the peak size

The peak-size forecast is a set of 23 quantiles. These form a median $\mathrm{med} = q(0.5)$ and 11 central prediction intervals $[L_\kappa, U_\kappa] = [q(\alpha_\kappa/2), q(1 - \alpha_\kappa/2)]$, $\kappa = 1, \dots, 11$, with $\alpha_\kappa \in \{0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, \dots, 0.9\}$; the interval $[L_\kappa, U_\kappa]$ has nominal level $1 - \alpha_\kappa$. (In this subsection $y$ denotes the observed peak count $C^*$.) For an observed value $y$, the **interval score** of a central $(1-\alpha)$ interval $[L, U]$ is
$$
\mathrm{IS}_\alpha(L, U; y) = (U - L) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(L - y)\,\mathbf{1}\{y < L\} + \frac{2}{\alpha}(y - U)\,\mathbf{1}\{y > U\}.
$$
The first term penalizes width, and the other two penalize the outcome falling outside the interval, more heavily for narrower nominal intervals (smaller $\alpha$). The **weighted interval score** (Bracher, Ray, Gneiting and Reich 2021) with $K_{\text{int}} = 11$ intervals is
$$
\mathrm{WIS}(q; y) = \frac{1}{K_{\text{int}} + 1/2}\left( \frac{1}{2}\,|y - \mathrm{med}| + \sum_{\kappa=1}^{K_{\text{int}}} \frac{\alpha_\kappa}{2}\, \mathrm{IS}_{\alpha_\kappa}(L_\kappa, U_\kappa; y) \right).
$$
An equivalent form is easier to compute: $\frac{\alpha}{2}\mathrm{IS}_\alpha(L, U; y) = \ell_{\alpha/2}(y - L) + \ell_{1 - \alpha/2}(y - U)$ and $\frac12 |y - \mathrm{med}| = \ell_{1/2}(y - \mathrm{med})$, with $\ell_\tau$ the pinball loss of @sec-gbqr, so
$$
\mathrm{WIS}(q; y) = \frac{1}{K_{\text{int}} + 1/2} \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} \ell_\tau\bigl(y - q(\tau)\bigr) = \frac{2}{23} \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} \ell_\tau\bigl(y - q(\tau)\bigr),
$$
twice the mean pinball loss over the 23 levels, which is how `score_peak_forecasts.py` computes it. WIS is a proper score for quantile forecasts, and as the number of quantiles grows it approximates the CRPS. It decomposes into three interpretable parts: **dispersion** (the width terms $\frac{\alpha_\kappa}{2}(U_\kappa - L_\kappa)$), **overprediction** (the penalties when $y$ falls below the intervals, together with the median term when $y < \mathrm{med}$), and **underprediction** (when $y$ falls above). Because counts differ by orders of magnitude across locations, WIS is computed both on the count scale $C^*$ and after applying $\log(1 + \cdot)$ to both the forecast quantiles and the observed count; relative measures (a model's mean WIS divided by the baseline's over the same forecasts) are also useful.

## Interval coverage and median error

The empirical **coverage** of the central $(1-\alpha)$ interval is the fraction of forecasts for which $L \le y \le U$. For a calibrated forecaster it should be close to $1 - \alpha$. We report 50% coverage ($[q(0.25), q(0.75)]$) and 95% coverage ($[q(0.025), q(0.975)]$). We also report the relative error of the median, $q(0.5)/\max(C^*, 1) - 1$, as a descriptive summary.

## Oracle outputs and the tie rule

Scores require the true values, which `build_peak_oracle.py` derives for each evaluated season and location:

- **Data.** The weekly target `wk inc flu hosp` in the sandbox's `target-data/oracle-output.csv` (NHSN counts as of 2026-07-08). "Final" therefore means that vintage; values from the most recent season may still be revised, which is noted when reporting results.
- **Peak.** $C^*$ is the maximum over that season's 34 pmf dates in `hub-config/tasks.json` (@eq-peak-size), and $W^*$ the earliest date attaining it. Only location-seasons with all 34 weeks present are kept.
- **Ties.** If the maximum is attained in more than one week, the location-season is flagged and excluded from peak-week scores, following FluSight's tie rule; its peak size is still scored.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Scoring details** (`score_peak_forecasts.py`). A submitted pmf is aligned to the 34 window dates (missing dates count as 0) and renormalized before scoring; the log score guards against $\log 0$ with a floor of $10^{-300}$. Each forecast row is also labelled with its distance to the true peak, $(r - W^*)$ in weeks (`weeks_from_peak`).
:::

## Development and test design {#sec-dev-design}

NHSN has only a few usable seasons, and all of them have already been looked at (the hindcasts of 2023/24–2025/26). Choosing among model variants by their NHSN scores would therefore overfit the choice to those seasons. Model development is instead done on a source that the NHSN forecasts never have to predict:

- **Development seasons: state-level ILINet in 2018/19 and 2019/20**, the last two full seasons before COVID-19 (`validate_ilinet.py`). No NHSN data are used at all. For development season $s$, a model is trained on every season before $s$ of ILINet (nation, HHS regions, states) and FluSurv-NET. It then forecasts the peak week and peak size of every state's ILINet series (about 46 states) at 29 weekly reference dates (season weeks 14–42, late October to mid-May). At reference date $r$ it uses only weeks through $r - 7$, since ILINet for a week is published the following Friday. Forward chaining means that the 2019/20 fit also uses 2018/19.
- **Real-time data.** ILINet has no vintages in `iddata`, but the Delphi Epidata API keeps every weekly release (unweighted ILI from the 2017/18 season on, clinical-lab positivity from October 2018). `epidata_ilinet.py` reconstructs the ILINet × positivity series of each state and the nation as published by each reference date (`validate_ilinet.py --realtime`). Weeks at least 10 weeks old are taken as final. Revisions are large: at first release the product differs from its final value by a median of 6–9%, with a 90th percentile of 45–65%, mostly because positivity is revised as more specimens are reported. Revisions go in both directions, unlike NHSN's mostly upward ones. Scores always use the final data.
- **Revision simulation.** With `--revisions`, the same block-bootstrap revision model as for NHSN (@sec-revision) is fit, at each reference date, to the ILINet revision vectors known by then. Revisions are measured against the latest value available at that date, with an offset of 0.01 in ILINet units and no strata. The model is then applied to 200 simulated final versions of the current season. Before about mid-December 2018 fewer than 200 revision vectors exist, and a symmetric perturbation with lag-0 SD 0.25 is used instead. That value was chosen with knowledge of the revision sizes above, a mild use of hindsight that affects only the first reference dates of 2018/19.
- **Other differences from the NHSN setting.** State ILINet also has about eight earlier seasons per state, whereas NHSN has two or three, so features that use a location's history (`hist_rel`) and location effects are better informed here than they will be for NHSN. Peak size is in ILINet units and is scored with WIS on the $\log(y + 0.01)$ scale; the log score and RPS for the peak week are as defined above.
- **Test seasons: NHSN 2023/24 and 2024/25.** The few variants that do well on the development seasons are then run as real-time NHSN hindcasts (@sec-dev-design-test) and compared with `peak_baseline`, `peak_gbqr` and `peak_kcde`, the models already hindcast on NHSN. No model developed since then has been run on NHSN yet (@sec-future). 2025/26 is left for a final check, keeping in mind that the earlier models were already examined on it.

## Development results {#sec-dev-results}

::: {.callout-warning title="Two development seasons only"}
State-level ILINet in 2018/19 and 2019/20 (about 45 states, 29 reference dates each; @sec-dev-design). With two seasons, differences of a few hundredths in mean log score are within season-to-season noise. None of these versions has been run on NHSN.
:::

All numbers are means over states, reference dates and both seasons (`analysis/peak-models/ilinet-validation/scores.csv`, rows with `agg_level == "state"`). Higher log scores are better; RPS and WIS are lower-is-better and are shown relative to the baseline in the same setting (below 1 is better than the baseline).

### Real-time data matter

The same baseline model, scored three ways:

| Setting | Log score | RPS | log-WIS | 50% cov. | 95% cov. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Final data (not real time) | −1.50 | 1.30 | 0.284 | 0.70 | 0.94 |
| Data as published, taken at face value (`@rt`) | −1.83 | 1.40 | 0.296 | 0.54 | 0.79 |
| As published, with revision simulation (`@rtrev`) | −1.66 | 1.35 | 0.292 | 0.58 | 0.92 |

In plain terms: forecasting from provisional data as if it were final costs a lot. The log score drops by a third of a unit, and the 95% intervals for peak size cover the truth only 79% of the time. Most of the damage comes from weeks that are later revised into, or out of, being the peak, which a model that trusts the provisional data gives only the floor probability. Simulating revisions (@sec-revision) recovers most of the loss. The remaining gap, compared with final data, is information that is genuinely not available in real time. All comparisons below use the real-time setting with revision simulation.
